title: Data protection & confidentiality
blurb: UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018 and the Caldicott principles: keeping patient information safe, and knowing when sharing is justified.
question: A man rings the practice saying he is a patient's husband. He asks what time her appointment is today and what treatment she's having. She is sitting in the waiting room. What can you tell him, and why?

teach.body: Patients tell the dental team things they may not tell anyone else: medical conditions, medicines, money worries, home life. If they can't trust you to keep it private, they stop telling you, and care becomes unsafe. Confidentiality is a professional duty (GDC Principle 4) and a legal one. UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 control how personal data is used, and health information is 'special category' data that needs extra protection. Even the fact that someone is a patient is confidential, and the duty continues after death.

teach.h: The UK GDPR principles in a dental practice
head: Principle
In practice
rows: Tell patients how their data is used (privacy notice)
Use data collected for care only for care
Collect and share only what is needed
Update medical histories and contact details
Keep records for the set period, then destroy securely
The practice can show how it complies
teach.caption: The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) is the UK regulator for data protection.

teach.h: Before you share: the Caldicott test

steps.label: Only if necessary
steps.sub: Could care go ahead without it?

teach.caption: There are eight Caldicott principles. The others: everyone must understand their responsibilities; the duty to share for care is as important as the duty to protect; and patients should be told how their information is used.

teach.h: When can confidential information be disclosed?

children.label: e.g. court order
children.sub: Refer to the dentist or IG lead

teach.caption: If none of these apply, don't disclose. Disclosures are made by the dentist or information governance lead, not on the spot by the nurse, and are recorded.

teach.body: Relatives have no automatic right to information, so a husband, wife or adult's parent needs the patient's consent. On the phone, confirm who you're speaking to before giving details. Respect contact preferences: don't leave a detailed voicemail or message at home unless the patient has agreed. Don't discuss patients in reception or the waiting room, and offer a private room for sensitive conversations. Lock or log off screens, keep day lists out of sight, and shred labels and paperwork rather than using the ordinary bin.

rows.label: Telling the dentist about a medicine the patient mentioned to you
Confirming to a caller that someone is a patient
Sending a referral letter with the details the hospital needs
Telling a patient's wife a diagnosis he wants kept private

teach.note: Information that matters for care must be shared within the team, even if the patient told only you. Confidentiality protects patients from outsiders, not from their own clinicians.

items.label: to respond to a subject access request (usually free)
to report a serious data breach to the ICO

teach.caption: Patients have a right to see their records (a subject access request). If data goes to the wrong person, such as a letter to the wrong address, that is a data breach: report it straight away under the practice procedure, who decide whether the ICO must be told.

teach.text: Being a relative is not the same as having a right to know. Unless the patient has consented (or someone has legal authority, such as a parent of a young child), you don't confirm appointments, treatment or even that the person is registered.

items: Health data is special category data under UK GDPR and the DPA 2018; the ICO is the regulator.
Share only with consent, when the law requires, or in the public interest (serious harm).
Caldicott: justify, necessary, minimum, need to know, lawful; sharing for care matters too.
No details to relatives or callers without consent; check identity on the phone.
Subject access: one month. Breaches: report internally at once; serious ones to the ICO within 72 hours.

summary: You can now explain why health information needs special protection, apply the UK GDPR and Caldicott principles, decide when disclosure is justified (consent, law or public interest), protect confidentiality at reception and on the phone, and respond correctly to access requests and data breaches.

A.q: A caller says he is a patient's husband and asks what treatment she is having today. What should you do?
options: Tell him, as he is her next of kin
Confirm the time but not the treatment
Give no details without her consent
Ask him to hold while you check her notes
A.why: Relatives have no automatic right to information. Without the patient's consent you shouldn't confirm details, even that she has an appointment.

whyNot.0: Next of kin has no legal right to a competent adult's information.
whyNot.1: Even confirming an appointment time reveals she is a patient.
whyNot.3: Opening her notes for him moves towards disclosure without consent.

A.q: Which Caldicott principle is applied when a referral letter includes only the details the specialist needs?
options: Use the minimum necessary information
Inform patients how data is used
Comply with the law
Everyone must know their responsibilities
A.why: Using the minimum necessary information means sharing only what the recipient needs for the purpose.

whyNot.1: That principle is about telling patients how their information is used.
whyNot.2: Compliance with the law matters, but the specific principle here is minimum necessary.
whyNot.3: That principle is about staff understanding their duties.

A.q: A letter containing a patient's treatment plan is sent to the wrong address. What is the first step?
options: Report it under the practice breach procedure
Wait to see if it is returned
Ring the wrong address and ask them to bin it
Send a second copy to the right address
A.why: This is a personal data breach. Report it immediately under the practice procedure so it can be assessed and, if serious, reported to the ICO.

whyNot.1: Delay could breach the 72-hour ICO reporting window.
whyNot.2: Contacting the recipient may help, but the breach must be reported first.
whyNot.3: Resending fixes the delivery but ignores the breach.

B.q: Under UK GDPR, how is information about a patient's health classed?
options: Public domain data
Special category data
Non-personal data
Low-risk routine data
B.why: Health information is special category data, which needs extra protection.

whyNot.0: Health information is confidential, never public domain data.
whyNot.2: Data about an identifiable person is personal data.
whyNot.3: Health data needs extra protection, not less.

B.q: A patient asks for a copy of her dental records. How long does the practice normally have to respond?
options: 7 days
40 days
Three months
One month
B.why: A subject access request must normally be answered within one month, usually free of charge.

whyNot.0: Seven days is not the legal time limit.
whyNot.1: 40 days was the limit under the old Data Protection Act 1998.
whyNot.2: Three months is too long; extensions apply only to complex requests.

B.q: A patient tells you privately about a new heart medicine but asks you not to 'make a fuss'. What should you do?
options: Keep it to yourself, as she asked
Tell the dentist, as it affects care
Write it down but tell no one
Tell reception to update her file later
B.why: Clinically relevant information must be shared with the treating dentist. Sharing within the care team is part of safe care.

whyNot.0: Keeping it secret could lead to unsafe treatment.
whyNot.2: The dentist must know before treating, not just find it later.
whyNot.3: Reception isn't the right route; the clinician needs to know directly.

C.q: Which situation most justifies sharing confidential information without the patient's consent?
options: A relative is worried about them
A colleague is curious about the case
A child is at risk of serious harm
A newspaper asks about a complaint
C.why: Disclosure can be justified in the public interest, such as safeguarding a child from serious harm, following the practice procedure.

whyNot.0: Worry doesn't override a patient's right to confidentiality.
whyNot.1: Curiosity is not a need to know.
whyNot.3: The media has no right to patient information.

C.q: Which is the best way to dispose of used appointment lists and patient labels?
options: The ordinary office bin
The paper recycling sack in the office
An orange clinical waste bag
Shredder or confidential waste
C.why: Confidential paperwork must be shredded or put in confidential waste.

whyNot.0: Anyone could read papers in an ordinary bin.
whyNot.2: Clinical waste is for contaminated items, not confidential paper.

C.q: A patient has asked the practice not to leave messages on her home phone. The dentist needs to rebook her. What should you do?
options: Leave a brief voicemail anyway
Use the contact method she agreed
Ask a family member to pass it on
Post a letter marked 'urgent'
C.why: Respect the patient's recorded contact preferences.

whyNot.0: This ignores her stated wishes and could reveal information to others.
whyNot.2: Passing messages through family breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.3: A letter may be fine only if she agreed to post; follow her preference.

reteach.title: Information is the patient's, not the practice's
reteach.question: Imagine every patient's details are in a sealed envelope with their name on it. Who can open it, and when?

blocks.body: The practice looks after the envelope, but what's inside belongs to the patient's private life. The care team may open it because they need the contents to treat safely. Anyone else needs a key: the patient's consent, a legal requirement, or a serious risk to someone (public interest). A worried husband, a curious colleague or a friendly caller has no key, however reasonable they sound.

blocks.caption: Caldicott: the duty to share for care is as important as the duty to protect.

blocks.text: Removing a name doesn't make information anonymous. A rare condition, a date, a street or a photo background can be enough to identify someone.

explain.body: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 govern personal data. Health data is special category data. The ICO regulates and enforces.

test.q: Which body regulates data protection in the UK?
options: The Care Quality Commission
The General Dental Council
The Information Commissioner's Office
The Health and Safety Executive (HSE)
test.why: The ICO is the UK's independent regulator for data protection.

whyNot.0: The CQC regulates care quality in England.
whyNot.1: The GDC regulates dental professionals, though confidentiality is also a GDC standard.
whyNot.3: The HSE regulates workplace health and safety.

explain.body: Default to confidentiality. Disclose only with consent, when the law requires it, or in the public interest where there's a risk of serious harm. Senior staff decide; it is recorded.

test.q: The police phone asking for a patient's address, with no court order. What should you do?
options: Give it, as the police always have authority
Refer the request to the dentist or IG lead
Refuse outright and end the call
Ask the patient's family first
test.why: Disclosure decisions go to the dentist or information governance lead, who will consider whether the law or public interest justifies it.

whyNot.0: A phone call alone doesn't create a legal duty to disclose.
whyNot.2: Refusing outright isn't right either; the request needs proper consideration by the right person.
whyNot.3: Family have no say over the patient's information.

explain.body: Check callers' identity, follow contact preferences, keep conversations private, lock screens and shred paper. Information goes only to those who need it for care.

test.q: A patient starts discussing a sensitive medical issue at the busy reception desk. What is best?
options: Carry on quickly to save time
Ask them to put it in writing
Offer a private room to talk
Lower your voice and carry on
test.why: Offering a private area protects the patient's confidentiality and dignity.

whyNot.1: Writing it down isn't necessary and may put them off.
whyNot.3: Quiet voices can still be overheard.

explain.body: Patients can request their records: respond within one month, usually free. A breach (wrong address, lost paperwork) is reported internally at once; serious ones go to the ICO within 72 hours.

test.q: Within what time must a serious personal data breach normally be reported to the ICO?
options: 24 hours
One month
7 days
72 hours
test.why: Reportable breaches must be notified to the ICO within 72 hours of becoming aware of them.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not the UK GDPR limit.
whyNot.1: One month is the time for a subject access request.
